analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on foreign profits corporations bring home if they keep or grow US jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and received no action after being referred to the Senate Finance Committee, dying there when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: US corporations had roughly $2 trillion in profits sitting with their foreign subsidiaries, untaxed because the money had not been brought home. This bill would let companies bring those profits home and deduct 75% of them, paying tax on only a quarter — an effective rate of about 8.75% instead of the 35% rate then on the books. To get an extra bonus deduction of up to 10%, a company would have to grow its US payroll above 2014 levels, and it would owe $75,000 for every full-time US employee it lost in the two years after taking the tax break.
analysis.who_benefits: US multinational corporations with large amounts of accumulated profits in foreign subsidiaries, who would pay a fraction of the normal tax rate on that money when repatriating it. Workers at those companies could gain indirectly if the payroll-growth bonus and job-loss penalty push companies to hire, though the strings attached are modest relative to the size of the tax cut.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets corporations deduct 75% of dividends received from their controlled foreign corporations, so profits brought home would be taxed at an effective rate of roughly 8.75% under the 35% rate then in effect, instead of the full 35%.

The measure revives a temporary provision last used in 2004-2005: the bill text updates the prior law's 2003-2004 reference dates to December 31, 2014 and applies to the last taxable year before enactment or the first year beginning within one year after.

Companies that grow their US payroll above 2014 levels earn a bonus deduction of up to 10% of the repatriated dividends in the following year, and companies that cut full-time US employment below their prior average over the following 24 months must add $75,000 to taxable income for each employee lost.

analysis.who_pays: The US Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers, would bear the cost of letting repatriated profits go untaxed at 75% — a large revenue loss. Companies with no offshore profits gain nothing, placing domestic-only competitors at a relative disadvantage.

drawbacks.text: The core of the bill is a large tax cut for companies with money offshore: a 75% deduction means the most profitable multinationals pay a fraction of the rate domestic businesses pay on the same income, and the Treasury forgoes the difference.

The employment strings are limited: the penalty counts only full-time US employees as classified by the employer's own standards, is capped so it can never exceed the value of the deduction, and the payroll-growth bonus is capped at 10% of the repatriated amount — far smaller than the tax break itself.

The bill's model, the 2004 repatriation tax holiday, is widely reported to have delivered most of its money to shareholders through buybacks and dividends rather than new hiring, which is why this proposal carries employment conditions the 2004 law lacked.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is an improvement on the 2004 holiday because it ties part of the benefit to keeping and adding US jobs, and the $75,000-per-job clawback gives companies a real reason not to lay people off. But the strings are small relative to the prize: the deduction is worth far more than any penalty or bonus, and the requirement is measured against a 2014 payroll baseline that acquisitions can inflate. On balance the bill transfers far more to corporations than it secures for workers, with the revenue cost borne by everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: McCain introduced the bill and it went straight to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill on February 5, 2015; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral, and the Congress ended January 3, 2017 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and ordinary taxpayers avoided forgoing the large revenue that the 75% deduction would have given away, and companies that would have enjoyed the low rate on offshore profits did not get it. Nothing changed for companies whose profits remain offshore, since the underlying tax treatment stayed as it was.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 5, 2015 and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a markup or committee vote; the bill received no action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and had only its Republican sponsor with no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: US multinational corporations with offshore profits
industries.note: They would pay an effective rate of about 8.75% instead of 35% on profits brought home — a windfall worth far more than any hiring bonus they could earn. The benefit would flow to companies and their shareholders, with the revenue cost spread across all taxpayers.

Companies without foreign subsidiaries would get no benefit while their multinational competitors received a steep rate cut on repatriated profits, putting them at a relative competitive disadvantage.
The 75% deduction would forgo a large amount of tax revenue that otherwise would have been collected when profits came home, leaving fewer resources for public spending or the need for other taxes.
